video_title: Treasury Markets not as “Safe” as You Think | Systematic Investor | Ep.414
gist: Mark Rzepczynski and Niels Kaastrup-Larsen catalogue a set of mid-August 'rumblings' — a 67% single-month blowup, a Korean equity bubble unwind, surging stock issuance, joint MOF/Fed yen intervention, a $15bn loss in Jane Street's situational-awareness fund, Moderna +177% in a day, and an LME copper spread squeeze — all occurring while VIX stays low. The core segment argues the US Treasury market is structurally less 'safe' than assumed: the Treasury's expanded buyback program (from ~$2bn to ~$4bn/month) is a signal that off-the-run liquidity is broken because primary dealer capital hasn't scaled with an ~$800bn-per-week auction calendar, leaving levered hedge-fund basis traders financed in repo as the marginal buyer. They close with the Arthur Sepp trend-following taxonomy, a tick-size explanation for why short-term trend fails, and a tribute to Victor Niederhoffer.

insights.claim: Mark Rzepczynski's read of markets in mid-August 2026 is that a cluster of unrelated stress events — a 67% single-month fund loss, the Korean equity bubble bursting after a huge run-up, a surge in new stock issuance with big reversals in the new issues, and yen intervention by both Japan's Ministry of Finance and the Fed — constitute 'rumblings' of an approaching storm rather than isolated accidents.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: A checklist of leading stress markers to monitor: leverage blowups, bubble unwinds, issuance surges, and FX intervention — each historically precedes broader repricing.
insights.quote: I'm seeing a lot of rumblings that are starting to bother me.

insights.claim: A rising pace of equity issuance is itself a valuation signal: heavy new-issue supply plus big reversals in those new issues is a classic marker of an overvalued market.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Track issuance volume and post-IPO reversal breadth as a free, high-frequency overvaluation gauge for equity beta exposure.
insights.quote: usually it's a sign of an overvalued market when there's more stock issuance

insights.claim: Official intervention in FX rarely works, so the fact that both Japan's MOF and the Fed intervened in the yen is more useful as information about official discomfort than as a reason to expect the trend to stop.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Intervention is a fade-or-follow decision point: trend followers can treat it as confirmation an imbalance exists rather than as a reversal signal.
insights.quote: Intervention usually doesn't work in the foreign exchange markets, but that hasn't stopped the governments to say like we've got to arrest the uh what is going on in the yen market

insights.claim: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen flags that the reported $15bn loss in Jane Street's situational awareness fund, against roughly $40bn of gains, points to unexpected position concentration inside firms marketed as diversified multi-strat pod shops.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Allocators should re-underwrite the assumption that many pods equals diversification; concentration can reassemble at the firm level.
insights.quote: 15 out of 40 is a big deal if it's happening on one bet.

insights.claim: Modern market makers are not the market makers of old — they run hundreds of speculative and hedging positions predicated on cross-stock correlations, so a correlation regime break turns a market-making book into a large directional loss.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Liquidity provision itself is now a correlation carry trade; when correlations break, liquidity withdraws exactly when it is most needed.
insights.quote: if the market starts to arrest and the correlations that we thought existed in the past don't exist currently, that could lead to a lot of profit losses

insights.claim: Single-stock volatility now materially exceeds typical futures volatility — Moderna rose 177% in one day and Micron went from roughly the high 300s in April to about 1,200 — which makes newly listed single-stock futures a meaningful new risk source for systematic managers used to index-level moves.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen and Mark Rzepczynski
insights.so_what: Trend programs adding single-stock futures need gap-risk sizing far beyond their futures-calibrated vol targets — a short in a 177%-gap name can be an account-level event.
insights.quote: Maderna went up 177% in a day

insights.claim: Despite the accumulating stress signals, realized and implied volatility remain low and geopolitical uncertainty has come off its Ukraine-war highs — the danger is in complexity and ambiguity, not in the VIX.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Cheap optionality: with vol depressed while structural fragilities build, convexity is available at low cost.

themes.theme: Commodity inventories as the real driver

insights.claim: Inventory and buffer-stock levels, not price trend alone, determine whether a commodity curve flips from contango to backwardation and whether the front end turns whippy — extreme moves happen when the warehouse buffer is exhausted and a producer must pay any price to keep a production line running.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Overlay inventory/days-of-cover data on price trend signals to anticipate curve regime shifts before they show up in flat price.
insights.quote: Looking at inventory levels is critical to understand whether there's going to be a change from contango or to backradation

insights.claim: The LME copper story is not the flat price but the spot-to-three-month spread, which blew out to extreme levels on the biggest weekly inflow to LME sheds since 2020 before partially retracing in the last 24 hours — still elevated.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Spread and warehouse-flow data are giving a squeeze signal that outright copper price does not — relevant to anyone trading front-month copper futures.
insights.quote: copper squeeze draws biggest weekly flow to LME shed since 2020

insights.claim: China has been suppressing global oil prices by drawing down its own strategic inventories rather than buying in the market, deliberately protecting the economic growth that sustains its trade-surplus engine — making China the swing consumer whose buffer exhaustion, not Middle East headlines, is the real oil risk.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: The bullish oil catalyst to watch is Chinese inventory depletion, which converts a suppressed market into a blowoff — argues for owning cheap upside calls rather than chasing headlines.
insights.quote: as you draw down your inventories, and this is also in the US, if we have our uh our oil reserves, this is that then you don't have any more buffer stock. Then what? Then then you have the real big blowoff price

insights.claim: The 2024-style cocoa episode is the working template for what happens when inventory simply is not there — the same mechanism now applies to metals warehouses.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Historical analogue for position sizing: inventory-driven squeezes produce multiples, not percentages.

insights.claim: Niels notes that guest Adam Rosenswag argues roughly a billion barrels of physical oil are unaccounted for, a setup that could resolve in much higher oil prices — with timing, not direction, being the open question.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: A large missing-barrels discrepancy is an asymmetric setup: the trade is long-dated optionality rather than a timed spot position.

themes.theme: Treasury buyback as a distress signal

insights.claim: US Treasury weekly auction volume can approach $800 billion during refunding weeks, much of it rollover, which makes the Treasury Secretary's self-described role as the world's number one salesman for US bonds a genuine structural constraint rather than rhetoric.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Auction absorption capacity is now the binding constraint on long-end yields — watch bid-to-cover and dealer takedown as the leading indicator.
insights.quote: we could be uh auctioning off close to $800 billion in a given week, which is astounding number

insights.claim: The Treasury has expanded its buyback program from roughly $2 billion to roughly $4 billion a month to repurchase illiquid off-the-run bonds and reissue on-the-runs — changing the composition of the debt, not its quantity.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Small in dollar size but large in information content — it confirms officially that off-the-run liquidity has deteriorated enough to require intervention.
insights.quote: now they've been increased from about 2 billion to about 4 billion uh dollars a month

insights.claim: The real message of the buyback program is that there is no longer enough market-making power to keep off-the-run Treasuries liquid — the Treasury is signaling a liquidity problem it cannot fix through the dealer system.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Read the buyback as an admission of dealer balance-sheet scarcity; expect wider off-the-run/on-the-run spreads to persist and widen further in stress.
insights.quote: there isn't enough market making power to be able to en ensure that these off-run bonds have enough liquidity. And that's where the real problem is.

insights.claim: Niels notes the buyback was announced the day after the 30-year Treasury hit 5.34% — the highest in years — which invites the reading that authorities have found their pain point on long-end yields, close to soft yield-curve control.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: If 5.34% on the long bond is the revealed policy pain threshold, it becomes a tradeable ceiling to lean against until official capacity is exhausted.
insights.quote: the timing of it uh kind of the day after the Treasury long bond hits 5.34% which is like the highest we've seen in god knows how long seems a little bit suspicious

insights.claim: Rzepczynski's operating premise for reading official announcements is that reassurance is itself a warning sign — when a government tells you not to worry, that is the moment to start worrying.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: A reusable filter for policy communications: weight the existence of the statement more than its content.
insights.quote: if the government tells you not to worry that's the time to start to worry

insights.claim: This buyback is a Treasury action, not a Fed action — distinct from QE composition shifts and distinct from the Yellen-era strategy of shortening average maturity by leaning on bill issuance to avoid pushing long rates up.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Three distinct levers act on the long end — Fed balance sheet, Treasury maturity mix, and buybacks — and conflating them leads to mispricing which authority is actually constraining yields.

insights.claim: The open question is what the Treasury swaps into when it buys back 14- to 27-year paper: if it funds repurchases with bills rather than 30-years, that quietly becomes long-end pressure relief and the start of something much larger than the current drop-in-the-bucket size.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Monitor the maturity composition of reissuance after each buyback — a shift toward bills would be de facto curve management with real duration-supply consequences.
insights.quote: The size that they're talking about is a sort of a drop in the bucket. But all of a sudden, this is that you sort of say that if you know offrun treasuries start to get prices that are, you know, out of out of line

insights.claim: With the buyback the Treasury effectively becomes a discretionary bond-market stabilizer, stepping in to buy off-the-runs it deems cheap relative to where it thinks the curve should be.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: A new price-insensitive marginal buyer with a view on fair value changes the relative-value distribution for anyone trading the off-the-run curve.
insights.quote: they're actually act acting as uh bond market stabilizers, albe it's a very small program

themes.theme: Treasury plumbing: dealers, hedge funds, repo

insights.claim: There is no exchange for cash Treasuries — the market is over-the-counter and run through Fed-designated primary government securities dealers whose available capital has not scaled with the size and volume of the Treasury market, in part because of supplementary liquidity ratio regulation.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Dealer capacity is the choke point; any SLR relief or tightening is a direct, tradeable input to Treasury liquidity and term premium.
insights.quote: there may not be enough capital at primary government security dealers for them to do their job to make markets

insights.claim: When a dealer cannot warehouse a bond, the adjustment shows up as a wider bid-ask spread and longer inventory holding periods that require financing — so capital scarcity translates mechanically into worse execution for every Treasury seller.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Execution costs on Treasuries are a function of dealer capital, not of the credit of the issuer — budget for slippage that scales with stress.

insights.claim: Hedge funds now hold over 9% of total marketable Treasuries and may exceed mutual funds as holders — the marginal buyer of the long end has shifted from unlevered real-money accounts to levered accounts.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: The single most important structural change in the Treasury market: the marginal price-setter can be forced to sell by a margin call, not by a view.
insights.quote: We're looking at 9% plus of the total of you know tradable uh marketable treasury bonds

insights.claim: Per Fed studies, the number one hedge fund trade in Treasuries is the cash-futures basis trade, which means anyone trading Treasury futures is very likely trading against a basis trader arbitraging against the cheapest-to-deliver.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Futures market liquidity is transmitted into cash Treasuries through levered basis traders — so a futures shock propagates straight into cash pricing.
insights.quote: the number one trade is the basis trade

insights.claim: Because basis trade profits are only a few ticks in a liquid market, the trade only pays if leveraged enormously through repo — so what looks like a low-risk, low-return arbitrage is in fact the most levered position set in the Treasury market.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Repo haircuts and rates are the real risk control on the Treasury market; a small change in financing terms forces large deleveraging in the cash bond.
insights.quote: the only way you're going to make any money at the basis trade is that you've got to use a tremendous amount of leverage on what you think is a fairly low risk low return trade that you lever you lever up like crazy

insights.claim: Because the marginal Treasury buyer is repo-financed, anything that hits repo — Fed balance sheet reduction or a rise in short rates — spills into the bond market through channels that are not well understood.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Overnight funding conditions are now a leading indicator for long-end Treasury dislocations — watch SOFR spreads and repo volumes as an early-warning system.
insights.quote: whatever happens to the repo market is going to spill over to the bond market in ways that we're not really sure of

insights.claim: A growing share of Treasury market making is done by electronic HFT firms such as Citadel that do not report to the Fed and carry no market-making obligation — they can simply switch off in stress.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Observed Treasury liquidity is conditional and can vanish without notice — depth in calm markets is not a measure of depth in stressed markets.
insights.quote: if they say like, I don't think this is a really good time to be involved in treasuries, they could just turn off the computer and that'll have an impact on the rest of the market

insights.claim: March 2020 is the proof of concept: Treasuries did not behave as the safe asset, and safety must be defined as both getting paid and being able to sell at a fair price when liquidity is needed — by the second definition Treasuries no longer clearly qualify.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: If Treasuries fail as a crisis hedge again, the entire risk-parity and 60/40 construction premise breaks — argues for alternative crisis diversifiers such as trend following.
insights.quote: we expected that treasuries would act as a safe asset and it didn't act like the safe asset

insights.claim: Niels compares the Treasury basis-trade setup to the EUR/CHF peg trade that everyone loved until the Swiss National Bank released the franc — a crowded, levered, low-volatility position whose risk is entirely in the discontinuity.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: The historical analogue implies the Treasury basis unwind, when it comes, is a gap event rather than a drawdown you can trade out of.

insights.claim: Niels frames the deeper issue as a slow, cyclical erosion of institutional trust, arguing that markets can operate with a lot of structural fragility until confidence goes — at which point the adjustment is not gradual.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Trust is the non-linear variable: fragility metrics can look stable for years and then reprice all at once.
insights.quote: once you lose the trust of the market uh then uh all hell breaks loose

themes.theme: Trend performance and the setup for autumn

insights.claim: As of 18-19 August 2026 the trend complex was up mid-single digits for the month and near double digits for the year: BTOP50 +1.78% MTD / +9.87% YTD, the trend index +1.69% / +9.73%, and the short-term traders index +1.37% / +4.6%, with traditional assets also strong — S&P 500 total return +2.97% MTD / +12.6% YTD and MSCI World +2.63% / +12.3%.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Trend has kept pace with equity beta year to date while offering different risk — relevant to allocators considering the crisis-hedge question raised by Treasury fragility.
insights.quote: we have the Btop 50 up 1.78% for the month of August. Uh up 9.87 for the year.

insights.claim: US aggregate bonds gained 72 basis points in the days around the Treasury buyback announcement but remain up only 0.39% for the year — a reminder that the fixed income asset class has delivered almost nothing in 2026 despite the recent rally.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Flat-for-the-year bonds combined with liquidity fragility weakens the case for bonds as the primary portfolio diversifier.

insights.claim: Niels's trend barometer has cooled to a neutral 43, indicating trend breadth in the tracked portfolio is neither unusually broad nor unusually narrow — consistent with a few days of correction in trend positions, especially in fixed income.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Neutral breadth means no crowding signal either way — the trend opportunity set is average, not stretched.

insights.claim: Rzepczynski expects a strong trend environment into the autumn specifically because ambiguity is high — the yen carry unwind is incomplete and Fed policy direction is unclear given Treasury financing moves — and ambiguity forces investors to revise expectations, which is what produces trends.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: A causal, not correlational, argument for adding trend exposure now: uncertainty about policy is the raw material of persistent directional moves.
insights.quote: there's a lot of ambiguity and and ambiguity means that people are going to be cautious that they're going to have to adjust their expectations and that's going to lead to trends

insights.claim: The yen intervention is evidence of an unresolved macro imbalance in currency markets rather than a resolution of one, implying the carry unwind still has room to run.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Positions the yen as a candidate for a multi-month trend rather than a mean-reverting intervention fade.

insights.claim: Arthur Sepp's updated 'art and science of trend following' paper classifies trend followers into three families: European (high signal-to-noise entries with continuous dynamic position adjustment), American (breakout entries with digital, all-in positioning), and academic time-series momentum (scaling continuously between positive and negative returns).
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: A concrete due-diligence taxonomy for differentiating managers that otherwise all describe themselves as trend followers.
insights.quote: he sort of said that there are three class classifications uh we'll call it the the European American and we'll call it classic

insights.claim: Niels pushes back that the 'American' breakout-with-static-sizing label describes how the US industry started rather than how it operates today — many US firms, including his own, now use dynamic position sizing.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Geographic labels in manager taxonomies are stale; diligence should verify actual sizing mechanics rather than accept the classification.

insights.claim: The three trend styles produce broadly similar Sharpe ratios and drawdowns and all perform well in strongly trending periods — the differences determine when each does relatively better or worse, not whether trend works.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Style selection is a second-order decision; the first-order decision is having trend exposure at all.
insights.quote: you need to have trend followers no matter what style you have and if there's a big move it doesn't matter you'll do well

insights.claim: Because the future path of markets is unknowable, Niels argues manager portfolios should be built on structural differences — number of markets traded, speed, methodology — rather than on picking the style you expect to win.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Practical allocation rule: diversify along structural axes you can observe, not along forecasts you cannot make.

insights.claim: The optimal number of trend followers in a portfolio has been studied and is smaller than for other hedge fund styles — you need more than one for style diversification but you do not need ten.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Concentrating a CTA sleeve in a handful of structurally different managers replicates the benchmark without the fee and operational drag of a long roster.
insights.quote: the number of trend followers you need to be able to replicate a benchmark or replicate is probably less than for some other hedge fund styles

insights.claim: Managers tend to stay wedded to the single trend style they launched with out of human conservatism, and the next evolution of the industry is single firms blending multiple pure-trend methodologies inside one program.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Style-blending inside a program is a source of edge and a diligence question to ask incumbents who have not changed models in decades.

insights.claim: Rzepczynski proposes the 'podification of trend following': run American breakout, European dynamic, and time-series momentum as separate internal pods, net their signals before execution to cut transaction costs, but track each pod's performance separately.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: An operating model that captures multi-manager diversification without multi-manager cost — a plausible template for how the next generation of CTAs is built.
insights.quote: I'll create a new word the podification of trend following

insights.claim: The bigger advantage of internal style diversification over hiring three to five separate managers is performance-fee netting, since the blended program reports one return stream — in Niels's view a materially larger benefit than the transaction-cost saving.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Quantifiable allocator edge: netting risk in a multi-manager CTA sleeve is a real, recurring cost that a single blended program eliminates.
insights.quote: you get netting of the performance fee. um because it turned it shows up as just one return stream

insights.claim: New research attributes the failure of short-term trend following to tick size: where ticks are very small, high-frequency market makers can add and pull orders fast enough to offset the gains short-term trend tries to capture, while contracts with large tick sizes still support profitable short-term trend.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: A screening rule for building short-term systems: rank the tradeable universe by volatility-adjusted tick size and only run fast models where the tick is wide enough to defend.
insights.quote: those that have very tight or small tick size, it is very hard to make profits in those markets

insights.claim: Niels clarifies that the relevant variable is volatility-adjusted tick size, not raw tick size — the ratio of tick to typical price movement is what determines whether HFT can arbitrage away the short-term signal.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Corrects the metric: normalize tick size by realized vol before using it to select markets for fast strategies.

insights.claim: Rzepczynski's stated research priority is market plumbing rather than modelling — tick size, who the players are in Treasuries, who is getting financing — on the view that these structural details, not the choice between a 50-day and 100-day breakout, determine outcomes.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Where the remaining edge sits for systematic managers: parameter tuning is commoditized, plumbing knowledge is not.
insights.quote: the plumbing matters in terms of all of this

insights.claim: Niels doubts that 'short-term trend following' is trend following at all — the firms in that space largely run volatility breakouts with exit rules unrelated to price reversal, so the label conflates two different return sources.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Allocators using short-term trend for trend-like crisis convexity may not be buying what they think — check the exit logic, not the entry.

insights.claim: Rzepczynski credits Victor Niederhoffer, who died in the past month, as one of the earliest true quant traders in the hedge fund space — a non-academic with academic chops who produced first-mover research on the headline overreaction anomaly, stock price clustering (the round number effect), short-term mean reversion after large moves, and insider-trading signals from executive buying and selling.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Several widely used systematic factors trace to one practitioner's 1960s-onward work — useful lineage for anyone building anomaly-based models.

insights.claim: Niederhoffer's operating principle — 'if you cannot count it, you do not know it' — meant rejecting unverified financial advice, intuition, and media speculation in favour of rigorous statistical backtesting, a mantra Rzepczynski argues every quant and trend follower should adopt.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Process discipline stated as a testable standard: you are only as good as the quality of your testing.
insights.quote: if you cannot count it, you do not know it

insights.claim: Niederhoffer viewed markets through evolutionary biology as an ecosystem rather than as an efficient-market equilibrium — which is the same concept Rzepczynski now calls market plumbing.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Connects the episode's two halves: understanding who the participants are and how they are financed is the same discipline whether applied to Treasuries or to equities.
insights.quote: it's not so much markets are efficient but you have to look at what the ecosystem of markets and how they behave

insights.claim: The Niederhoffer–Taleb rivalry is framed as the defining methodological split in quant investing: the empiricist who follows the data versus the skeptic who argues historical and statistical data can be misleading — with Niederhoffer's late-1990s blowup and subsequent comeback as evidence for both sides.
insights.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski, co-host
insights.so_what: Every systematic program sits somewhere on this axis; knowing where yours sits explains which failure mode you are exposed to.

insights.claim: Niels notes that an unusual number of highly successful managers came out of or were influenced by Niederhoffer's firm, including Toby Crabel and the famously secretive Monroe Trout, alongside Rzepczynski himself.
insights.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen, host
insights.so_what: Talent-tree evidence that the empirical-research culture, not the specific trades, was the durable output of that shop.
